input:
This review examines the staffing position of the quality
laboratory, with particular attention to the balance between
overtime working and permanent headcount. The laboratory currently
employs 12 full-time staff, and over the course of last year
overtime working amounted to 7% of paid hours, a level that has
prompted the question of whether an additional permanent
appointment would represent a better use of resources. The option
under consideration is to replace half of the overtime with one
additional hire. Half of the overtime corresponds to 3.5% of paid
hours, and the hire who would absorb that work would cost $87k per
year fully loaded, a figure bundling the salary and the associated
employer costs, charged in every month of the year.

A closer look at the pattern of the work, however, reveals a
significant complication. The overtime is not spread evenly across
the calendar but is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when
submissions arrive faster than they can be cleared, while between
the peaks the existing staff carry the workload within ordinary
hours. An additional hire, by contrast, is paid for the full year.
The laboratory would in effect be paying $87k during the off-peak
months, when the additional capacity is not required, to remove
overtime that arises only in the peak months. The comparison is
therefore between a fixed cost spread across the whole year and a
variable cost incurred in only part of it, and on the figures
available the variable arrangement remains the smaller commitment.

Taking all of this into consideration, the recommendation is that
laboratory management should hold staffing at its present level,
continue to cover the two peaks with overtime, and revisit the
question only if the peaks should lengthen or merge, since a
longer peak would change the balance on which the present figures
rest. The hire is not dismissed on its merits as additional
capacity; it is set aside because its cost runs for the full year
whereas the need it would answer runs for only part of it.
target:
Holding the present staffing is the cheaper course, and it is the
recommendation of this review. The quality laboratory employs 12
full-time staff, and last year it met its workload with overtime at
7% of paid hours. The proposal under review would replace half of
that overtime with one additional hire. Half of the overtime is
3.5% of paid hours, and the hire that would absorb it costs $87k
per year fully loaded: salary and the employer costs that ride on
it, charged in every month of the year.

The difficulty is the shape of the work. The overtime is
concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when submissions arrive faster
than the laboratory can clear them, and between the peaks the
present staff carry the workload within ordinary hours. A hire is
paid for the full year. The laboratory would therefore pay $87k in
the off-peak months, when the additional capacity is not needed, in
order to remove overtime that arises only in the peak months. The
trade-off is a fixed cost spread over the whole year against a
variable cost incurred in part of it, and on the figures available
the variable cost is the smaller commitment.

Laboratory management should hold staffing at its present level,
continue to cover the two peaks with overtime, and reopen the
question only if the peaks lengthen or merge, or if the workload
between the peaks grows beyond what ordinary hours can carry,
because either change alters the balance the figures rest on. The hire is not rejected
on its merits as capacity; it is rejected because its cost runs for
the full year while the need it answers runs for part of it.
